speechtext:
Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. 23, respecting foreign enlistment.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the second reading of the bill does not call for any discussion because the principle of the measure is already the law of Canada. The terms of the British Foreign Enlistment Act have always applied to Canada, therefore the principle is already accepted in this country. The purpose of the bill is to have a Canadian act, because under the Statute of Westminster any dominion, including the Dominion of Canada, may reenact, repeal or amend any statute already applying to it. It has been thought advisable and proper to have a Canadian act, known as the Foreign Enlistment Act, 1937, and to make the very few changes adapting it to Canadian conditions, especially changes which will make it applicable to modem air and land conveyances, as well as to sea conveyances, to which the original measure was limited. I suggest that the bill be read a second time and that any suggestions with reference to its provisions be made in committee.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. H. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) has said that the principle of this 'bill has been accepted by Canada. I think that principle was imposed upon Canada by imperial statute without any reference whatever to the will or opinion of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: But it applies to Canada.

Yes, it applies to Canada, but it was imposed rather than accepted. Although the British North America Act of 1867 purported to declare that the exclusive legislative authority of the parliament of Canada extends to all matters coming within certain classes of subjects mentioned in section 91 of that act, it was nevertheless soon ascertained that the Colonial Laws Validity Act, enacted two years previously by the parliament of the United Kingdom without any reference to the legislatures of Canada or of the maritime provinces, effectively restricted the field of Canadian legislation. Section 2 of that act of 1865-leaving out the unimportant words-* reads:
Any colonial law which is or shall be in any respect repugnant to the provisions of any act of parliament extending to the colony to which such law may relate . . . shall be read subject to such act . . . and shall to the extent of such repugnancy but not otherwise be and remain absolutely void and inoperative.
1940	COMMONS
Foreign Enlistment-Mr. Cahan
A few years ago I asked for a return from the Department of External Affairs showing the existing statutes of the parliament of the United Kingdom which extend to this dominion. This return was only partly prepared and for that reason was not laid upon the table of the house. From personal research I tabulated scores of such statutes which then and still apply to Canada, although under the act of 1867 they are now within the legislative jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada. The Statute of Westminster, 1931, provides as follows in section 2:
(1)	The Colonial Laws Validity Act, 1865, shall not apply to any law made after the commencement of this act by the parliament of a dominion.
That is after 1931.
(2)	No law and no provision of any law made after the commencement of this act by the parliament of a dominion shall be void or inoperative on the ground that it i9 repugnant to the law of England, or to the provisions of any existing or future act of parliament of the United Kingdom, or to any order, rule or regulation made under any such act, and the powers of the parliament of a dominion shall include the power to repeal or amend any such act, order, rule or regulation in so far as the same is part of the law of the dominion.
After the enactment in 1931 of the Statute of Westminster this parliament proceeded to revise the Canada Shipping Act. This monumental work was the first step by way of amending or revising imperial statutes which had hitherto restricted the operation of statutes passed by this parliament, and which had also restricted the effective expression in legislation of the will of this parliament. There are certain of these imperial acts which are and always have been assumed to be within the sphere of the parliament of the United Kingdom and with respect to which the parliament of the United Kingdom has assumed exclusive jurisdiction up to the present year. The parliament of the United Kingdom has assumed exclusive jurisdiction to regulate the succession to the throne, the titles of the crown, the royal declarations on accession and the regency in certain cases, as shown by the Demise of the Crown Act, 1901, the Regency Act of 1910 and the Royal and Parliamentary Titles Act, 1927, which concern the whole empire.
I do not intend to refer particularly to these statutes at the present time. I wish only to express for myself and on behalf of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), who is unavoidably absent, approval of the action of the government in revising the Foreign Enlistment Act, 1870. That English act extends to all the dominions and hitherto
CMr. Cahan. 1
has regulated the conduct of all of His Majesty's subjects during the existence of hostilities between foreign states with which His Majesty has been at peace. Therefore we commend this action, not with particular reference to the special clauses of this bill, but with reference to the purpose and intent of the bill to take additional measures to exercise the rights of nationality and sovereignty which we believe are now inherent in the parliament of Canada. Times have changed and are changing and I think it is necessary	that	this parliament should
endeavour to express itself with regard to all these matters as an assertion of its sovereignty in all matters which are normally within its jurisdiction.
There are other acts of a like character. There is the Army Act and the Naval Discipline Act of the United Kingdom, both of which extend to the whole empire. All dominion forces serving outside of the dominion are subject to the provisions of the Army Act and the regulations issued thereunder. The parliament of the United Kingdom has also provided for the extradition of accused persons from one part of the empire to another for trial. There is, for instance, the Fugitive Offenders Act, 1881, which provides for the arrest in any dominion of any person who is accused of the commission of an offence in any other of the dominions. We have dealt partially with this matter in the Canadian act, which is chapter 81 of the revised statutes of Canada. I suggest that that act should be extended still further by the assertion by this parliament of its legislative competence to deal with these matters.
Then there is the Admiralty Offences (Colonial) Act, 1849, which conferred on dominion or colonial courts the power to deal with crimes committed in the territorial waters of the dominion or colony. The Territorial Waters Jurisdiction Act of 1878 makes provision with respect to offences committed by foreigners on foreign ships within the territorial waters of any dominion. The Naval Prize Act, 1864, and the Prize Court Act, 1894, provide for the constitution of prize courts in British dominions, colonies and possessions. The Slave Trade Act, 1873, for the suppression of the slave trade, extends to the whole empire and confers jurisdiction upon the vice-admiralty courts of the dominion.
There are other classes of cases which have the same special application to Canada and which restrict to a certain extent the legislative jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada. Such are the International Copyright Act, 1886, and the Geneva Convention Act,

Foreign Enlistment-Mr. Cahan
1911. A large number of these acts, which were passed by the parliament of the United Kingdom and with respect to which Canada has had up to the present no legislative jurisdiction by way of repeal or amendment, are not generally known. In the course of my professional practice I have had on one or two occasions to quote one or more of these acts of the parliament of the United Kingdom which are in force in this country, and I was astonished to find that the judges presiding in the courts had no idea that any such acts were in existence extending to and applicable to Canada.
Now that parliament has commenced the consideration of acts of the parliament of the United Kingdom which extend to and are applicable to Canada, I suggest that the Department of External Affairs or the Department of Justice or both should proceed at once to make a complete survey of all such acts and determine which should be retained either in their present or in an amended form. If they are not amended and thereby included in the statutes of Canada they should be repealed by act of the parliament of Canada. Those not repealed should then be compiled and published in a special volume for ready reference, so that all concerned with the administration of the law may be fully informed as to what the law is. I suggest with deference that in a number of our courts, both in Quebec and other provinces, the judges are not fully aware of the extent to which the laws of the parliament of the United Kingdom apply to Canada and are to be enforced by our courts, both in civil and in criminal matters. I suggest also that if this work is too onerous and too extensive for the Department of External Affairs- which has one or two officials whom I know to be thoroughly competent for work of this kind-and if the Department of Justice has so much work in hand that its officials cannot devote the time necessary to a compilation of these enactments and to the preparation of amending statutes, it would be proper for the Department of Justice to employ some competent lawyer-I would not object if he were of the Liberal faith and persuasion so long as he is capable-to make a compilation of these laws and place them before parliament in a way in which they can be effectively dealt with. In an address I made to this house some time about 1928, dealing with this matter, I stated, if I remember correctly, that I had found over a hundred statutes of the United Kingdom which dealt with matters of this kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have a list of about one hundred and fifty.

Well, I remember that in the former discussion I said one hundred and fifteen, and my leader at the time remarked that on the previous occasion I had referred to the number as being about one hundred and fifty; but on this occasion, not having had the opportunity of reviewing the list, I referred to the smaller figure. I have no doubt that the number is over a hundred.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Of course many of them are the same measures, revised. For instance, there are many laws on the slave trade.

Quite so. The original act as amended is still in force. I suggest, therefore, very earnestly, that this matter be taken up. In expressing this opinion I think I may say that the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett)-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is a good suggestion.

-is entirely in favour of the suggestion which I have made. In my opinion this parliament should again and again, at every opportunity, assert its sovereignty in regard to matters affecting the peace, order and good government of Canada which are within its legislative jurisdiction. We have emerged from the colonial status, whether the judicial committee of the privy council recognize the fact or not; and, when they decline to recognize it, it is absolutely necessary in the present temper of this country that they be brought to a condition of mind in which they cannot avoid cognizance of certain fundamental facts. One way of doing that is to proceed as I have suggested, although there are cumulative remedies which on an appropriate occasion I shall take pleasure in expounding in this house from my point of view. I have simply to say that I approve the principle of this bill.
There is one matter which I might mention now, and which I think will require further consideration. This bill is a criminal statute. It provides penalties for certain crimes. It also proceeds to deal with nationals of Canada who commit these breaches of the law. To mention that fact is to revert to a consideration which I have very much at heart, and that is the necessity and the advisability of an amendment and consolidation of the laws of Canada relating to Canadian nationality. In the consideration of the provisions of the treaty of peace at Versailles dealing with reparations and other matters I was brought face to face, week after week and month after month, with the fact that this parliament has never clearly expressed tne meaning of Canadian nationality nor decided
1942	COMMONS
Foreign Enlistment

Mr. Cahan
the qualities which apply to a Canadian national. Following up some work which had been done under the present prime minister before I came into office in 1930-he procured a professor of the law department of the university of Toronto to prepare a report in connection therewith-I attempted the preparation of a bill on Canadian nationality and submitted it to this house. But I was unable to proceed with the matter, for the reason that, while the permanent officials of the various departments of government are intelligent and of ripe experience in the administration of their departments, their minds are very obtuse indeed to the reception of new ideas which concern general public policy in matters only incidentally affecting their departments. I ran up against barriers which I could not overcome, and I was unable to accomplish what I had sought, the enactment of a comprehensive measure setting forth the qualifications of a Canadian national and the definition in express terms of Canadian nationality. I repeat that sometimes I fear we have more of the colonial spirit of inferiority than even our fathers and grandfathers had, and certainly the time has come in the history of this dominion when, if we seek to ascertain who are Canadians and who are Canadian nationals, we should be able to find it in some substantive enactment outside of the immigration act, the real purpose and intent of which is to exclude certain classes of people from obtaining domicile in Canada. Why we should be compelled to look to that act for a definition of who are Canadians, who are Canadian nationals, I cannot understand. I think it is a discreditable condition in which we find ourselves to-day. Canada has taken an important part in international affairs. Under -the imperial conference resolutions of 1923 and 1926, and again at the imperial conference of 1930, we assumed a large part in the administration of external affairs relating to Canada. But we are now met by that same old imperial spirit, as expressed by certain members of His Majesty's Privy Council of England, who cannot understand that men of English descent and men of French descent whose forbears have been living in Canada for a century and more, and who are Canadians to the backbone, are not of the same inferior mental complex as all colonials were deemed to be a century and a half ago. The sooner we assert the sovereignty of Canada in all matters with which this parliament is competent to deal, the better I think it will be for this country -far better for the development of that national sentiment in Canada, which is absolutely necessary if we are to maintain cohesion 
among the various races and creeds and all sections of the dominion.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
speechtext:
With respect to a bill of this importance there seems to be no good reason why there should not be a full discussion on second reading. I regret that the government has introduced the measure at this time. At least in its present form, it may easily involve us in those European entanglements which ostensibly it seeks to avoid. Personally I am in favour of neutrality, but that neutrality must be thoroughgoing.
It seems to me that this bill has not been drawn with any great care. I do not know whether the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) is responsible for it: I am not reflecting upon him.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We cannot please the hon. gentleman.

We are told that the Foreign Enlistment Act passed by the parliament of the United Kingdom in 1870 extends to Canada. I submit that the government might have done one of three things. They might simply have repealed that act as far as it extends to Canada; or they might have reenacted it just as it stood, as applying to Canada; or they might have improved upon it. In my opinion the bill as drawn is no improvement upon the British act; rather in addition to the principle underlying the British act it introduces one or two other principles that make it quite involved.
We are in favour of what I think is the principle of the bill, at least the principle of the British act, that is, to prohibit military assistance to the enemies of a friendly state. The explanatory note to section 3, which I take it indicates the principle of the bill, reads:
This section makes it unlawful for a Canadian national to enlist anywhere, or for any person within Canada to induce any other person to enlist in the case of a foreign war, for service against a friendly state.
This undoubtedly involves control over our own nationals, and though we have not had many occasions on which to assert that control, I suggest that on the whole we must concede that at any rate, when the actions of Canadian nationals may involve us in international complications, the state must take control, or assume some power over their actions. The bill provides-I am inclined to think this is the original bill

for certain permits. Let me read section 3:
If any person, without a permit, being a Canadian national, within or without Canada, accepts or agrees to accept any commission or

Foreign Enlistment-Mr. Woodsworth
engagement in the armed forces of any foreign state at war with any friendly foreign state, or, whether a Canadian national or not, within Canada, induces any other person to accept or agree to accept any commission or engagement in any such armed forces, such persons shall be guilty of an offence under this act.
This idea of permits is carried into the other sections as well. By this provision for permits I suggest that the government is given power virtually to nullify the purpose of the bill by allowing the very things which it is intended to prohibit. It must be noted that the bill itself makes no reference whatever to the conditions under which such permits may be issued.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Does not my hon. friend think that that question should be discussed in committee? To show him how much better it would be to leave to the committee stage the discussion of such points I may tell him that certain things will be omitted from the bill.

I want to discuss
the principle of the bill as briefly as possible.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is
not the principle.

It has to do with
the principle of the bill because certain important matters are left to the discretion of the government-a procedure to which we are opposed. Further, there is a similar objection to section 19. This is important and should not be passed over at this stage. Section 19 reads:
(1) The governor in council may, from time to time, make orders and regulations relating to any or all of the following matters:
(a)	the extension and application of the provisions of this act, with necessary modifications, to any case in which there is a state of armed conflict, civil or otherwise, either within a foreign country or between foreign countries.
(b)	the issue of permits, the prescribing of conditions upon which permits may be issued, and the designation of the authority or authorities who may issue permits.
And so on. It strikes me that this government should be the last to advocate government by order in council. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said a few weeks ago, as reported at page 249 of Hansard:
Over and over again we have laid down the principle that so far as participation in war is concerned, it will be for the parliament of Canada to decide. Having taken that attitude with respect to participation, I think we might well take the same attitude with respect to neutrality.
I suggest to the government that this bill be brought into conformity with the principles laid down by the Prime Minister. The powers given to the government by section
19 to extend the provisions of the act are too wide, and certainly undefined. This is a delegation not to regulate but to legislate. Power should be given to apply the provisions of the act, not to extend them.
Further, in the event of civil war in a foreign country the act should be made to apply only when there has been prior recognition by his majesty's government in Canada of the insurgents as belligerents.
There is another point-and while it might be appropriately dealt with when we reach the relevant section, I think it is important to refer to it while discussing the purpose of the bill and the situations for which provision should be made. If enlistment, recruiting, and outfitting and use of ships are not permitted in aid of the armed forces at war with any friendly state, why should not the ban be extended to the sale of arms, munitions and implements of war or material essential to the manufacture thereof? In this connection I should like to quote a summary of the United States neutrality bill as approved by the senate. This summary is from the Montreal Gazette of March 4, 1937:
As soon as he should find that a state of war existed or that a civil war of such dimensions as to threaten the peace or neutrality of the United States was in progress, the following steps would automatically result:
1.	An embargo would be placed on all shipments of arms, ammunition and implements of war, and all loans to all belligerents and to all factions in civil strife.
2.	It would be unlawful for United States citizens to travel on ships of belligerent registry, except under such regulations as the president might prescribe.
3.	All trade with belligerents would go upon a "cash-and-carry" basis. No goods of any kind could be shipped to them from this country except after all right and title therein had been transferred from American nationals to foreigners.
4.	American ships could not legally transport to belligerents commodities designated by the president, presumably in accordance with belligerents' own proclamation of contraband of war.
We have before us a bill which no doubt is intended to keep us out of European difficulties. But we are simply prohibiting foreign enlistments; there is no thoroughgoing prohibition of arms and munitions. There is a mention in one case of ships, but prohibitory action is not extended to munitions of war.
A second principle emerges, which is quite different from the principle of the British act. It is contained in section 11, which makes it illegal to recruit or accept any commission or engagement in the armed forces of any foreign state, thus going much farther than the British act. Section 3 prohibits any-
1944	COMMONS
Foreign Enlistment-Mr. Woodsworth
one from enlisting against a friendly state, but this goes farther and makes it illegal to recruit or accept any commission or engagement in the armed forces of any foreign state. Why should not prohibitions which -are directed against assistance to states at war with friendly states also apply against assistance to rebels against a friendly state? An anomalous situation results. If I may quote the words of a friend who wrote to me with regard to this matter, he said:
All recruitment or inducement to enlist in favour of a friendly foreign power immediately becomes unlawful under this section. There is not even the qualification "without a permit" which applies to the unlawful action under section 3 dealing with aid to an enemy of a friendly state. The effect of section 11 is that while recruitment in aid of the armed forces of a friendly state is unlawful, recruitment in aid of the rebellious forces within the state is lawful.
Who is the author?
I am stating it as my own. The memorandum is from a friend who wrote me in regard to this matter. This is a technical matter; I am not a lawyer, and for that reason I am using the words as given.
It might have more force if we knew who wrote it.

No, I am letting the statement stand on its own merits.
Such an act is not forbidden by section 3, because it is not recruitment for a foreign state at war with a friendly power.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Again if my hon. friend would wait we might change this section to satisfy him.
I am very glad to hear it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I thought I told the hon. member I would.
No, there is still another section.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Ai speech having been prepared, it has to be delivered.

No, it is not because it was prepared and has to 'be delivered. That remark is hardly fair. On account of the importance of the subject I did give some study to it, and asked, one or two of my legal friends to advise me in regard to certain sections, and I think it is only fair that I should present the case at this stage, because the bill has to be considered as a whole; unless we give consideration to sections 11 and 19 we can hardly deal with the important section 3.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Why not wait until we reach those sections?

Well, as I have already said, there are two or three principles involved.. I wonder if I might be permitted to proceed for a few minutes more. I continue this statement:
Such an act is not forbidden by section 3, because it is not recruitment for a foreign state at war with a friendly power. It is not forbidden by section 11, because the enlistment is not "in the armed forces of the foreign state." Recruitment in aid of the armed forces of a friendly power is at all times unlawful, while recruitment in aid of the armed rebels within such a friendly power is lawful, and remains lawful unless power to declare otherwise is secured under section 19(1) (a). It is dubious whether such power is secured under 19(1)(a).
There is one other section which I think is very important. Section 14 takes away trial by jury. The explanatory note states that it is designed to enable the prosecuting authority to proceed1 summarily in the manner provided by part XV of the criminal code, in cases of minor importance. I suggest that this is not a matter of minor importance.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This I will not change.

Well, I regret that we should here be deprived of the right of trial by jury in a very important matter. I hope the government will see its way clear to accept such amendments as will clarify the situation and provide for thoroughgoing neutrality, and that parliament, not the governor in council, shall decide whether our nationals shall engage in. war.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I wish to thank the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) for the illuminating address he gave this afternoon on the various enactments and statutes which apply to Canada. I thoroughly agree with him that the present anomalous situation should be remedied, and I believe his suggestion that this should be made a special undertaking is a good one. I do not know whether the advisers in the Department of External Affairs and the Department of Justice can do it properly in the limited time at their disposal, but someone will have to do it. I agree entirely with everything my hon. friend has said in that respect.
As far as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) is con-

Foreign Enlistment
cernedi, he says he is in favour of the principle of the bill, and I am pleased that he is. But I cannot agree with his statement that the bill permits things which should be prohibited, that it will make it easier to do things which should not be done. I understood my hon. friend to say that instead of restricting, the bill would permit certain things to be done.
If I may say so, I was dealing with section 3 and the following sections which contain the words "without a permit."

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If my
hon. friend could see the hundreds of telegrams I have received from people who are opposed to this bill he would see that they are not objecting because it gives them more freedom to enlist for service in European wars.
Would the minister explain the meaning of the words "without a permit"?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We used those words because they are in the British act. They used the word "licence," but now the League of Nations has changed it to "permit," and that is the word we are using. The act would be made more rigid by removing those words "without a permit" in the various sections. So far as I am concerned I have no objection to that change. It will take away some flexibility, some elasticity in given cases which we cannot foresee, perhaps, but it may be better for the government not to be asked to issue permits; if they have not that power it will make it easier for them. So when the sections in question are reached I will move that those words be deleted. Meanwhile we will have to change section 2 accordingly, by striking out subsection (a), and another change may be required following the discussion of the other sections of the bill. I will ask that section 2 stand in the meantime.
Shall section 1 carry?

Has the minister decided
that the government should not be able to license an enlistment under section 3, for instance? Certainly under the act in force throughout the British Empire since 1870 licences could be granted, and I can conceive of circumstances and conditions under which a licence or permit might hereafter be issued.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think so, too.

I can conceive that. The government of the day must be responsible; it has to assume responsibility in such matters. I did not follow the reasoning of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in that respect. I think in a statute of this kind a certain amount of elasticity is necessary if justice is to be done under all circumstances and conditions.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 2-Definitions.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I will ask that this section stand and that the question raised by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George be discussed on the other sections. I may say that my mind is open on the question, and I should like to hear the reasons that may be given in support of the request of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
Section stands.
On section 3-Offence to enlist with a foreign state at war with a friendly state.

I do not know that I can do more than repeat what I have said already. If it is to be made illegal, as I think it should be, to enlist in the armed forces of any foreign state at war with a friendly state, I do not see why there should be any provision for a permit to do otherwise. It seems to me if that is to be illegal provision should not be made for the government to go against its own act. There should be no exemption at all. I can see no reason for a permit to enlist in the armed forces of a state at war with a friendly state.

Let me give an example. In the republic of Brazil we have had a large number of Canadian engineers professionally engaged in carrying out great undertakings. Yet by its own military law, unless that law has recently been changed, Brazil assumes the right forcibly to conscript the nationals of other countries temporarily domiciled in that state, and to compel such foreign subjects to take part in the wars of that state, either domestic or with another state. I am putting an extreme case, but should we visit upon such Canadian nationals the penalties imposed under this act? Should we say that they are committing a crime when they are forcibly enlisted by another country?
If it is done under duress it would hardly come under the provisions of this section, which says " accepts or agrees to accept."

Well, he accepts; he has to. This section says " Every person without a permit who accepts or agrees to accept any commission or engagement-."
Foreign Enlistment
Surely that means a voluntary action.

My hon. friend takes that as meaning a purely voluntary action. Well, I doubt that, but let me go further. Under the English act licences were seldom granted, but throughout the years they have reserved the right to license British subjects to take part in foreign wars.
Against a friendly state?

There is hardly a war to which they do not send representatives of their own staff to participate. Russia and Japan were friendly states, yet the British government sent members of its own staff to participate not only in the naval conflicts but in the land conflicts as well in that war. They do that in every great war. There must be some latitude allowed; you must not make it so rigid that there is no possibility of allowing exemptions in individual cases.
Did the members of the general staff participate as combatants in the wars to which the hon. gentleman has referred?

They certainly did; on
occasion they had to in order to preserve their own lives.

With regard to the argument of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, staff observers accompanying some army are not there because they have enlisted in the forces of that foreign state. A staff officer acting in the capacity of an observer is something very different from a man who has enlisted or accepted enlistment in the services of that state. It seems to me that if we leave a loophole through which permits may be given which will nullify the very intent of the act, we will set a dangerous precedent. As I understand it, the clause in the British act with reference to licences was inserted at the time of the Franco-Prussian war, at a time of imperialistic expansion, when perhaps there was more interference in the wars of other countries than there is to-day. The whole situation has changed now, particularly with reference to Canada, whose desire to keep out of international entanglements is even stronger than the desire that existed in Great Britain in 1870. It seems to me we are setting a very dangerous precedent if we leave any loophole through which by the issuance of permits or licences, individuals or groups of individuals may be permitted to enlist in the service of a foreign state.

Medical officers from Montreal are at present enlisted with and engaged

as part of the royalist service in Madrid. They are rendering surgical and medical aid and assistance, and form part of the forces and of the medical service of an army. Should that be prohibited?

That would depend entirely on the definition of "armed forces." Paragraph (c) of section 2 says:
(c)	"Armed forces" includes military, naval and air forces or services, combatant or noncombatant.
We are waiting to see what the minister has to say with reference to the definition of armed forces. I do not think the term "armed forces" has ever applied to the Red Cross or to medical services rendered in some other country for purely humanitarian reasons.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: To medical services, yes.
In the last war the Swiss forces helped both sides. The Red Cross is recognized as a non-combatant.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, the Red Cross, but not the medical staffs of armies.
I believe people rendering humanitarian or medical services on either side-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, it is strictly limited to the Red Cross.

That depends entirely on the definition of "armed forces." If we want to preserve the right to any country to send medical units to render humanitarian services, we can do so by dealing with paragraph (c) of section 2, rather than leaving in the words "without permit," which would cover military units.

I think it is important that such medical units be under the control of the Red Cross, that relief of the suffering be impartial and that it apply not only to one side. I cannot agree with the contention put forward by hon. members on the other side. If you attempt to define insurgency arising in any particular state you are apt to get into very serious difficulties. The section is well worded, and I have no doubt the Minister of Justice has given it serious consideration. I assure my hon. friend that I am not speaking without careful consideration, and I have such advice from men of experience in the legal profession; it is their opinion that an addition such as the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) has suggested, should be made. This is a permanent statute, and it places too much responsibility on the government to assume discretionary powers with regard to civil conflict within another nation. As to the definition of civil conflict, one in the form proposed by my colleague would, I suggest, meet the situation. I think that the inconsistency of the section as it stands is clear. This is one of the governing sections of the statute. It is unlawful for me to enlist in the armed forces of a foreign state at war with another foreign state, yet it continues to be lawful for me to enlist in the armed forces of insurgents within a friendly foreign state. Surely the inconsistency must be apparent. It is not so much a question of legal technicalities as a matter of common sense. The minister apparently pins his hope to a definition under section 19 of the jurisdiction of the government in such matters, but I refer him to the terms of section 19, which gives discretionary powers. It is extremely dangerous to attempt to exercise discretionary power, or to define without bias what is civil conflict, when the government is actually confronted with a state of civil conflict. Inasmuch as we are dealing with a permanent statute it is essential to give a proper definition, and " rebellion " or " insurgency " or " insurrection "-any of those terms could be used. They are clearly understood; they are defined, I understand in international law, and the inconsistency can easily be removed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

press and some legal gentlemen claimed that the Foreign Enlistment Act did not apply to a case of civil war. In international law it is not as clear as he suggests. I could quote precedents on both sides. It is extremely difficult to ascertain when the trouble has become an insurrection that is recognized by other countries.
Then there are conditions under which war practically exists without having been declared. We saw that situation in China and Japan a few years ago in connection with Manchukuo, and then we saw it in Ethiopia. Italy did not declare war on Ethiopia; she described it as a territorial adventure, or expansion. That is one of the main reasons why it is important that the government should be given the power which we seek in section 19, to be able at a given point to declare that a conflict, such as the trouble in Manchukuo, in Ethiopia or elsewhere, has developed to such an extent as to be a threat to the peace of other nations. At such a time it will be for the governor in council to apply the provisions in this act to a conflict of that sort and prohibit Canadians from taking part in it.
In my opinion the bill as drafted covers everything, and my hon. friend's suggestion instead of helping would make it more difficult because it would not then be for the governor in council, in the light of the conditions that might exist at the time, to apply the act to a particular armed conflict. The question whether armed forces are insurgent or are government

forces depends upon the recognition by Canada of a state as the government or of the forces as insurgent. That may change in the twinkle of an eye; it is a matter within the discretion of the government of the United Kingdom in any case. We might have a long discussion as to how far recognition would be within the discretion of the government of Canada under a recent decision, but circumstances change from day to day, from week to week, and the government must always be at liberty to determine whether a sit-down strike in any foreign country is an insurgency or whether it has reached that stage when rioters have become an insurgent force.
I am speaking of armed insurgency.

The sit-down strikers seem to be armed in most cases. At any rate some of their deeds result in conflict, and whether they carry bludgeons or pistols does not decide the issue. There must be a discretion vested in the government.

I do not think that without knowledge of the actual conditions and the facts you can draw a line. If you have a government in this country you must give it authority to exercise a certain discretion in complicated cases. You cannot tie down by a rigid statute the government's decision in every complicated case that may arise in international affairs. You must have a government that takes responsibility. You cannot call this parliament together simply because a question arises as to whether a certain band of insurgents, although armed, should be regarded thereafter as the loyalist forces. Parliament cannot be convened on every such occasion, and you must give the government of the country discretion. If you have a government which you are confident will not exercise proper discretion the sooner you vote against it the better; but there is human frailty everywhere, even in governments. In drafting a statute such as this you must assume that the government of your country will exercise a reasonable discretion in dealing with such matters in accordance with the exigencies of special occasions as they arise.

Provided, however, that the provisions of this section shall not apply to the action of foreign consular or diplomatic officers or agents in enlisting persons who are nationals of the countries which they represent, and who are not Canadian nationals in conformity with the regulations of the governor in council.

The difficulty has arisen chiefly in view of the fact that certain foreign states do not recognize certificates of nationalization granted in Canada. The result was that, as Secretary of State, for four or five years I declined to grant certificates of naturalization to aliens resident in Canada and otherwise qualified, unless they obtained from the foreign government to which they formerly paid allegiance a certificate' of the renunciation of their allegiance. I believe any regulations made should be very severe indeed. Propaganda such as has been carried on in the last few years is most injurious and prejudicial

to the development of a Canadian national spirit among those immigrants from foreign countries who are domiciled in Canada, many of whom in times past have applied for and obtained certificates of naturalization in Canada.

Foreign language communities.

In some sections of Canada there are considerable numbers of Italians, and in other sections we find Germans, Ukrainians, and persons of other nationalities. criminals of these representatives, but I think their activities should be circumscribed within certain limits by regulations of the governor in council.

It means that many people are placed in an awkward situation I had a man come up to my room the other day who is from my own constituency. He came to Canada in 1923 from a country in Europe. My advice to him was to take out Canadian naturalization papers, but he had not gained a domicile in any particular locality because of his movements. It does not seem right to me that a man who has lived in Canada and who intends to make his future home in this country should be bothered in this way. This is one of the sections to which I called attention when I spoke on the second reading. It practically takes away the right of trial by jury. It permits the prosecuting attorney to proceed summarily in the manner provided by Part XV of the criminal code. The crime which we are creating here is not a minor crime, and a man faced with a serious crime should have the fullest possible protection.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. member would make the treatment more lenient?

The difficulty is that on occasions such as this there is bound to be a division of opinion as to the issue involved. Undier our system, where the jury must be unanimous, it would be almost impossible to obtain a conviction. If it is left to a judge, the judfee will decide the case strictly in accordance with the law. For instance, there is a definite cleavage in opinion right across the continent with regard to the civil strife in Spain. I am old enough to remember our boys in western Nova Scotia coming back from the civil war in the United States in a condition much worse than those who came

Foreign Enlistment
back from the war in Europe. Anaesthetics were not known or used at that time. In western Nova Scotia, where I was born and bred, the young men went out and enlisted in the northern army, while the sailors along the shore served in ships which were running and evading the blockade against southern ports. These ships were carrying cotton to England, where it was sold in the textile markets at enhanced prices. In a war of that kind, there is bound to be a decided division of domestic sentiment. I can remember how as a lad I used to go to the post office every night and wait until nine, ten, or eleven o'clock to get the latest daily paper which came in by coach, in order to see the progress of the Franco-Prussian war. We were watching the progress at Gravelotte, and Sedan and were interested in what the communists were doing in Paris. The whole community was divided in sentiment. There were staid and sober citizens who would gladly have fought on one side, while other equally staid andl sober and religious citizens would have gladly fought on the other. I think it would! be just as well to have these cases withdrawn from the jury and decided by a judge in strict accordance with the law.
Would not that argument apply against all trials by jury?

No. I have had considerable experience in years past in a professional capacity, and I think I can say that with very few exceptions the great body of our people are in favour of proper and impartial administration of our criminal law.

What is meant by summary prosecutions? Does that mean that the case will be dealt with by a judge sitting in a criminal assize, or will it be considered by a magistrate in police court or by two justices of the peace?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Under part XV of the criminal codie it could be dealt with by a magistrate or by two justices of the peace.
This is a very serious offence, the offender being liable to two years' imprisonment. I think we should make sure that the man will be brought before a judge as we understand! the term.

speechtext:
The
accused would always have the right of appeal to a judge of a superior tribunal. There are many sections of the code which provide for trial in this manner, and offences under the customs act are treated in the same way.

To recognize their status, what they are or what they are not, would seem to me to be arrogating to ourselves a little too much importance, and, more particularly, to be intervening in things which do not concern us to that degree. It strikes me that under this section the government might even impound a passport on suspicion, if they deemed it expedient. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If this
were only a legislative gesture I might agree with the hon. member. But it is a serious matter. We do not want our people to go abroad and fight in these conflicts, and one of the best ways to prevent them is through the control of passports. Of course, a young Canadian may slip across the border in order to enlist in one of these armed conflicts, and if he cannot be caught before he leaves Canada, there is a reasonable expectancy, if we are empowered to interfere with the passport, that he will be stopped somewhere en route. One case was that of a young man in my own constituency who succeeded in getting a passport upon a member of the clergy agreeing to be responsible for him, but who afterwards stated that his assistance had been obtained by false representations. We cancelled the passport. Another man, named I believe Leclair, obtained a passport under somewhat similar circumstances and got as far as France; he was there arrested, and can proceed no further with that passport.
If we do not have the power contained in this provision there will be many who will certainly evade this legislation. The hon. member says it is an invasion of liberty. Salus populi suprema lex: the state does not desire to be involved in difficulties. I believe the JMr. E. Lapointe.]

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It reads:
But shall not include medical, nursing and other services engaged solely in humanitarian work and which are under the control or supervision of the Canadian Red Cross or other recognized Canadian humanitarian society.
The word "solely" applies to "humanitarian work."
There would still be provision for a medical unit which had not been endorsed by the Canadian Red Cross but which was engaged solely in humanitarian work?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, it would have to be under the control and supervision of the Red Cross.

Does that mean that all medical units now operating in Spain, unless within the next few days they receive the endorsation of the Canadian Red Cross, would not qualify under this clause, and that Canadians so engaged would be indictable under this act?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They are excepted now. This is not retroactive; it deals with those who may go from now on.
No.
But must those already there discontinue their work the moment this bill is passed?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, that is not the intention.
But is that what the bill Says?

I think the remarks of the minister, coupled with those of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan), make it necessary that we should have a clear understanding of the situation. These people left Canada on their own initiative, without the slightest thought that they would become offenders under a measure of this kind. Evidently they secured passports and thus left with the sanction of the government. At that time the Canadian Red Cross society had not organized any units to carry on humanitarian work in Spain, and these people associated themselves with similar groups in the United Kingdom. So at the present time, serving perhaps on both sides, we have eminent Canadian surgeons whose reputation for humanitarian endeavour is beyond question. As the bill now reads, and according to the opinion of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, if they continue in this humanitarian endeavour without securing the endorsation of the Canadian Red Cross, as soon as they return to Canada they are liable to indictment and imprisonment.
[Mr. Douglas.)

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I assure my hon. friend that that is not the case. Certainly no man engaged in humanitarian work in Spain at the present time will be indicted under this act because he is there now.

But in the circumstances under which they went abroad they had to attach themselves to the armed forces of one side or the other, though of course not as combatants. Those in command will not allow any persons except members of their armed forces to penetrate their lines even to alleviate the sufferings of the wounded.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
What is the objection to having them work under the Red Cross? The Red Cross is in Spain at the present time, carrying on its humanitarian activities on both sides. Why should there be any objection to coming under the Red Cross? I have in mind a resolution of the League of Nations, at its last assembly, dealing with this matter. Part of that resolution reads:
Notes that there are problems of a humanitarian character in connection with the present situation, in regard to which coordinated action of an international and humanitarian character is desirable as soon as possible-
The article from the convention, which I read a few moments ago, is also to the effect that such work should be impartial and international, and that it should apply to both sides. We have a splendid organization in the Canadian Red Cross society, which is affiliated with the International Red Cross committee, which is subject to certain rules and regulations, and surely Canadians who sympathize with the wounded and who want to give their money for that purpose might do it through this noble channel. I do not see the objection to it.
Do I understand that if they are not under the Canadian Red Cross, by reason of relationship entered into before the Canadian Red Cross became active, they will not be indictable under this act?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, not those already there, but I would say that surely from now on those carrying on this work should do so under the Red Cross.
I would ask the minister to insert the word "surgical" before the word "medical"; I think there is a clear distinction between surgical and medical services.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Very well;
I agree to that.

As I understand it, the object of the bill is to prevent individuals, firms, corporations or associations from exploiting for financial profit the names of these famous children. speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Is the house ready for the question?
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance):	I think that before the question is put, a statement is necessary similar to the one I made in the banking and commerce committee when Bill No. 57 was before it, in connection with which there was a discussion upon what had taken place in the house previously with regard to this class of bill.
I intimated to the banking and commerce committee that the government had received within the last few months a very largely signed petition, which I believe originated with some of the companies concerned with this class of business, asking for the appointment of a royal commission to inquire into the whole matter. I was able to indicate to the banking and commerce committee that the government had given consideration to the petition and that, in the light of the discussion of its subject matter in the house, the government did not deem it a suitable subject for reference to a royal commission but rather that it should be investigated by a special committee of this house assigned- to that particular task. I indicated last session the government's desires in this regard from the standpoint of gathering information in an effort to enable the house to reach a decision on policy. I also stated earlier in the session the reasons why in the judgment of the [Mr. Chairman.}
government the information was not as yet sufficiently complete to enable progress to be made.
During this year the superintendent of insurance will be asked still further to gather all available material in connection with the problem of small loans, and at the next session of parliament the government will ask the house to consent to the appointment of a special committee which will be charged with the investigation of the whole problem of small loans.
In the meantime the company concerned in the present bill has apparently taken cognizance of the proceedings in the banking and commerce committee and in the house and of the criticisms which have been levelled against it, and also of the action of the banking and commerce committee with, respect to the other bill, No. 57. I say that because I found on my desk this evening a letter from the Central Finance Corporation, reading as follows:
We hereby undertake and consent to amend our private Bill No. 58 (Letter C of the Senate) by reducing the rate to two per cent per month and altering the wording of the bill so as to make it conform to private Bill No. 57 (Letter H of the Senate) of Industrial Loan and Finance Corporation, except that section 1, changing the name, and section 2, increasing the capital stock, will be retained in our bill as at present.
Under the circumstances I am personally prepared to let this bill go to the banking and commerce committee. I am quite satisfied that in its previous form it could not have passed the banking and commerce committee, but having regard to the decision made on Bill 57 I think there is justification for sending this bill to the committee in the expectation that it will be amended in the same manner as the former bill, and bring about to that extent at any rate, a reduction in the maximum rate of interest and in the total charges which may be made by the company.

I do not desire to discuss this bill at any length to-night. The general subject which it covers has been debated on a former occasion in connection with a similar bill.
This company has a charter issued by the parliament of Canada and has operated for a considerable time under its provisions. It now comes to parliament and asks for some amendments. I know that parliament is seized of the importance of this question, and I am sure that if the bill is referred to the banking and commerce committee, with the information which that committee has and with its

Central Finance Corporation
disposition thoroughly to study and investigate the matter, the bill will be given that consideration which it deserves and which all bills receive when they go to a committee of this house charged with the duty of studying their provisions.
The subject is one upon which a great deal may be said on both sides, and I agree with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) that under the circumstances, and in view of what has taken place, the proper course for the house to adopt now is to refer the bill to the committee. In that committee both those who support the bill and those opposing it will have an opportunity to express their views. Moreover, I am sure the superintendent of insurance will be consulted as to the provisions of the bill. There, I have no doubt, full justice can be done to all parties concerned. I concur therefore in the suggestion that the bill be referred to the banking and commerce committee.
Miss AGNES C. MACPHAIL (Grey-Bruce): I am quite sure that the bill will be referred to the banking and commerce committee, but I do not think we should lose this opportunity of protesting not only against the bill itself but against the small loan companies that charge excessive interest rates. Two per cent sounds small, but actually it is two per cent per month, and it has been said that this comes to about 27 per cent a year. That is not interest, and for the life of me I cannot understand how people who cannot pay their debts can pay them plus 27 per cent per annum. I am therefore opposed to the bill on every count.
The government and parliament of Canada are no doubt aware that there are a great many people in this country who need loans; but those who need them most are the ones who can least afford to pay such exorbitant interest rates. I suggest that we ought to encourage credit unions which would help out people with small, steady salaries. They would help these people in this very way by making small loans at reasonable rates.
Frankly another reason why I am opposed to the bill is the lobbying that has been done for it. I do not mind anyone asking me to dinner, but not for the purpose of lobbying me in connection with a bill, and there are now in the gallery people who are paid substantial salaries and who have been spending money, which I judge is not their own, asking people to lunch. If there is anything I hate worse than another it is just that. If their bill is as good as we are led to believe they could have saved their money and the common sense of the house-because
there is a good deal of common sense scattered throughout the house-would have seen its virtue. Intensive lobbying is suspicious, and is a good reason why we should investigate very carefully any bill that is supported in that way.
There is only one reason why I should like to support the bill, and that is on account of its sponsor (Mr. Duffus). But one cannot allow friendship to carry one so far. I shall therefore vote against the bill on the general principle that such bills are wrong. The people who need loans most are being charged the highest rates of interest, and some provision must be made for them. It is true, information may be brought out in the committee; but if we allow this bill to go to the banking and commerce committee without protest and a division we consent to its principle, and I do not consent to the principle of the bill. I simply wish to register my objection and my reasons for it.

If gives me a good deal of pain to express an opinion in opposition to the hon. member who has just spoken (Miss Macphail). At first I was very much in doubt what I should do about this bill, and I have examined it with considerable care during the last few days- let me add, not as the result of lobbying. No one has invited me to lunch in connection with this bill.
In the first place I am very much opposed to high rates of interest; no one in the house is more opposed to such rates than I am. That fact would naturally prejudice me against the bill but for certain other considerations which in my judgment ought to be borne in mind. We must not forget that there are' people who simply must borrow; there is no doubt about that. Many times they need to borrow in case of death or an operation or because of some other unforeseen circumstance. For all these reasons people are forced into a position where they absolutely must borrow.
At present we have no provision for such people. Personally I favour the development of credit unions, but they are not yet developed. And what are we going to do for people who need to borrow between now and the time when the credit unions are in a position to help them? This government has made no arrangement whereby such people may obtain loans from $50 to, say, $150; and as far as I know, no province or municipality has any such provision; and as I say, the credit unions are not yet sufficiently developed. Where can these people go? There is only one bank that is in a position to offer personal

Central Finance Corporation
loans, and 'after looking into the situation with respect to that bank I find that the conditions under which it will make loans are prohibitive to a great many people who might need loans very badly. These are considerations that have greatly influenced me.
There is another matter that we must not forget. We became much in favour of prohibition at one time. We thought that by passing a law against liquor we should stop people drinking it. But they only went to bootleggers. That was entirely an unforeseen and unexpected result. Similarly, we know that people will borrow, and if we do not provide an orderly way in which they may obtain loans, they will go to bootleggers; and I am not at all convinced, after looking into the matter, that they will fare any better at the hands of bootleggers.
Some facts have been drawn to my attention with respect to this particular company, the Central Finance Corporation. I have not had time to investigate and find out whether all these things are true, but the following facts have been brought to my attention regarding the company and I submit them to the house for what they are worth. I must say, that when they tell us earnestly that these things are true, these things ought at least to be taken into consideration.
I understand that this company is at present carrying 30,000 borrowers. Manifestly there are 30,000 Canadians who have been in such a position that they have had< to turn to this company for assistance. If we prevent this company from carrying on, what will happen to these borrowers and those who would follow after them? I understand further that this company during the past four years has issued 86,204 loans, totalling $15,213,781, and that during that time this remarkable record has been established by that company: They have never seized any furniture or household goods, they have never garnisheed anyone's wages nor had recourse to court action. I do not know whether that is true, but if it is I consider it a very fine record.. I submit that in all justice this house should allow this company's doings to be investigated' by an impartial body with more time at its disposal than we have.
Here is another thing which impressed me greatly. It was brought to my attention that the average net profit of the three chartered personal loan companies in Canada for the years 1933, 1934 and 1935 was only 5-73 per cent. On the face of it, it looks like 27 per cent per annum, but when the company is making only 5-73 per cent net, it does not seem so exorbitant as at first I thought it was. I understand, further, that it has been calculated that if the reduced rate of 2 per cent

per month proposed in the present bill and Bill No. 57 is made effective, on the basis of the business of 1936 the net earnings of the company would be 4-97 per cent, which is not exorbitant.
Another feature is that passing this bill does not commit parliament to anything new; the principle has already been established. It only reduces the rate which is already permitted by parliament. And' when in addition to all these things I consider that we have already sent Bill No. 57 to the committee, the only fair thing to do is to send this one along the same road. I am in favour of sending this bill to the committee.

The hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) has just said that this company earns only a little over 5 per cent. That may be so as far as the shareholders are concerned, but it does not take into consideration the salaries of the executives and those behind the concern.
Referring to the rate of 2 per cent odd per month which figures up to approximately 27 per cent per annum, I understand that those who have to borrow money from these companies are people in great need of money and with very little security. I have understood from people who have gone to them that some companies have said: "We will charge you 3 per cent per month for your short term, but there is something more for which we must charge. We have our general overhead and office expense, for which we must add a percentage. Then we have our investigation costs to be taken care of, so we must add a percentage for that. Then we have losses with those unable to pay, which we have to write off; so we have to make another little charge for that." When it is all totalled up, it is not merely 2 or 2J per cent per month which has been charged, because the addition of all these costs runs it up to a very great amount.
There is another thing. When people find themselves unable to pay the company will say to them: Well, could you pay at some future time if we extend your note? Borrowers will try. If the loan was for say $50 the company will make it $75, and extend it for three months. That is something that this house should look into very carefully. I am entirely in favour of having this matter go to a commission and have them investigate fully the companies which are applying for these charters.

We
had a bill similar to this before the house a short time ago, and I voted against its being sent to the banking and commerce committee. I do not wish to appear to be sanctioning in

Central Finance Corporation
the remotest way the interest rates provided for in that bill or in this one; I am decidedly opposed to that. But inasmuch as the house has already permitted the other bill to go to the committee I am going to vote in favour of this bill going there. It may be that there it will be so radically changed in respect to interest rates that I might see my way to vote for it when it comes back to this house. But I shall never vote for any bill which permits the rate of interest provided for in the present bill. It may seem a paradox but I want it clearly on record that I am not sanctioning the interest rates provided for in this bill by voting that it go to the committee.
Mrs. MARTHA L. BLACK (Yukon): I intend to vote for this bill's going to the committee. We all know that even a criminal has the right to be heard before a judge and jury. I do not know that I approve of the interest rate, but I do approve of the bill being examined by the proper committee. I should also like to state that while I have had luncheon with one of the so-called lobbyists in the gallery, I do not feel that that luncheon purchased me. It is ten or twelve years since I had my first luncheon with that so-called lobbyist, and neither did that lobbyist intend to purchase me then nor did I intend to purchase her by the meals I have given her at different times. I shall vote for the bill's going to the committee.
I should like to say a word-
Tell us about the meal.
The only meals I have had so far are those I have had to pay for myself, unfortunately. The hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Miss Macphail) has offered to take me out for dinner-
That is bribery.

Very delightful bribery. I was glad to hear the Minister of Finance make the statement that he proposes to appoint a committee of this house to go into the whole question of small loan companies. Perhaps one of the most detrimental things in Canada to-day, from the standpoint of the small wage earner, is the small loan company.
In reply to the suggestion that we should let this bill go to the committee, I want to remind the house that Bill No. 57 also went to the committee, and it is now back for third reading. It seems to me that if we are to make any protest, this is the time to do so.
The arguments and statements presented by the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Black-31111-124
more), I have heard presented before, but I do not know just how much value they have. The hon. member stated that a large number of people must borrow. That is quite true, but those who must borrow are the very people who are not in a position to mortgage their future by paying interest at the rate of 27 per cent per annum. The argument, of course, is that we already have other loan companies charging exorbitant rates, and because this is so, we must legalize certain companies which will perhaps charge more moderate rates.
Someone used prohibition as an illustration. When we tried to prevent people from drinking intoxicating liquor they turned to bootleggers, and now the suggestion is that because we have loan companies which charge exorbitant rates of interest we should legalize other companies which perhaps will not rob the public to such an extent. In other words, because we have pirates we must now legalize some gentler form of piracy. It does not seem to me, Mr. Speaker, that by perpetrating a wrong we can hope to remove a great evil, and I should like to see this house take the stand that no action whatever will be taken with regard to this bill or Bill No. 57 until such time as a committee of this house has gone into the whole question of loan companies right across Canada.
The fact that there are thirty thousand borrowers from this company is something that hon. members should think about very seriously. When it is stated that this company is carrying thirty thousand borrowers, I think it is probably true that the thirty thousand borrowers are carrying the company. It is being carried by people all over the country who, from their small weekly earnings, are compelled to pay more than they can afford in order to meet interest charges.
One of the regrettable features of this whole question is that when a member of this house, for instance, or any one receiving an average income needs money in a hurry, usually he can go to the bank and borrow it at six or seven per cent. But a person who cannot afford to pay high rates of interest when he borrows money cannot get a loan for six or seven per cent but is compelled to pay this exorbitant rate of twenty-seven per cent. There is an old biblical saying that to him that hath shall be given, and from him that hath not shall be taken away even that which he hath. That is very true of borrowing. The man who can afford to pay a high rate of interest can borrow at a low rate, while the man who cannot pay a high rate is the very person who is compelled to do so.

Central Finance Corporation

While in the city of Chicago I spent some time studying in the court of domestic relations, and since that time I have had the privilege of sitting on the bench beside various judges in juvenile and domestic relations courts in order to make a study of juvenile delinquency and marital disputes. It is a safe prediction that a large percentage of the cases coming before the average domestic relations court is concerned with couples whose marital incompatibility is due largely to the fact that they are in straitened financial circumstances, due in large measure to their having borrowed money from some small loan company. Then, as the months went by, they got deeper and deeper into the toils of the company, with the result that there were disputes and bickerings that often led eventually to the divorce court.
I think it is criminal for us to condone in any form any bill that will legalize financial piracy in the Dominion of Canada, In my opinion, sending this bill to a committee, will simply result as in the case of Bill No. 57, in its being sent back here for third reading. If we have any thought at all for the small wage-earners of Canada, who have been and will become entangled in the toils of loan sharks, we ought to turn down this bill now rather than merely go through the motions of sweetening the poison and salving our conscience by putting the bill through a series of committees and then letting it slide through the house. I am opposed to this bill. I am opposed to its going to any committee until an investigation has been held into the whole question of small loan companies.

Mr. Speaker, I am not in the position of one who is forced to sing for his supper; I paid for my own. I think I know something about the principles involved in these bills. I have been somewhat entertained by the suggestion that the majority of people who are willing to pay high rates of interest for a short term loan are people in unfortunate circumstances. What little knowledge I have leads me to the conclusion that a much greater percentage of the money that is made in this kind of transaction is made at the expense of shorts in the market than at the expense of unfortunate people who need money for some emergency and who have to pay these interest rates. In most communities in Canada we have educated the people to the point where those who have to go into debt because of sickness or some similar reason know that funds will be made available to them. So I say that in my experience the major part of this money is loaned to people who have been caught in the market.
